“no me lo creo” = I can’t believe it
In -ía the stress falls on the i, and the two vowels are separate syllables: te-NÍ-a, vi-VÍ-a, co-MÍ-a.
The b in -aba is soft, between vowels: hablaba = “a-BLA-ba”, with the b almost breathed.
The Spanish imperfect covers two English structures: “used to” (habits) and “was …ing” (background). “Vivía” = “I lived / I used to live”, “jugaba” = “I used to play / I was playing”.
It’s one of the most regular tenses: almost every verb follows the rule, including tener (tenía), hacer (hacía), querer (quería), poder (podía).
“Yo” and “él” have the same form: hablaba. The context or the pronoun tells you who: “yo hablaba / ella hablaba”.
“Era” is easy to remember: think of an “era”, a period in the past.
“Había” (there was / there were) is the imperfect of “hay”: Antes había un cine aquí = There used to be a cinema here.
3. When do you use the imperfect?
Todos los días iba a la escuela.
Every day I went (used to go) to school.
La casa era grande y tenía jardín.
The house was big and had a garden.
Tenía diez años. Eran las tres.
I was ten. It was three o’clock.
I used to smoke, now I don’t.
Words that usually call for the imperfect: antes, de pequeño, cuando era niño, siempre, todos los días, a menudo, normalmente.
SOLER + infinitive describes habits. In the past: solía, solías, solía…
As a child I used to play in the fields.
On Sundays we used to eat with our grandparents.
It also works in the present (o → ue): Suelo levantarme a las siete = I usually get up at seven.
5. Imperfect or indefinido? A first look
Both are past tenses. The difference in simple words:
Imperfecto (how it WAS, what happened often)
Jugaba al fútbol todos los días.
Imagine a film: the imperfect is the SETTING (how everything was), the indefinido is the ACTION (what happened). We combine them in the next chapter.
“I used to smoke, now I don’t.”
A description in the past → imperfect.

Grandma Rosario tells her grandchildren what life was like when she was young.
When I was young, Madrid was very different.

¿Qué hacía el padre por la noche?
Mihai was born in a small village in Transylvania, thirty kilometres from Sibiu. He lived there until he was ten.
The village was very pretty. It had an old church, a small school and a single shop that sold everything.
The houses were colourful and they all had a garden with fruit trees.
Mihai lived with his parents and grandparents in a big house by the river.
His grandfather was a carpenter. Every morning he worked in his workshop, and Mihai watched him for hours.
His grandmother made the best bread in the village. On Sundays the whole house smelled of warm bread and cozonac.
In summer, Mihai and his friends swam in the river and played football until evening.
They had no video games and no phones, but they were never bored. They built huts in the forest and climbed trees.
In winter everything was white. The snow came up to the windows, and the school sometimes closed.
In the evenings the family sat by the stove, and his grandfather told stories about wolves and bears.
Mihai was a very curious child. He always asked why: why it rains, why birds fly, why people get ill.
One day his grandmother told him: “You’re going to be a doctor.” She was right.
Now, when Mihai is tired at the hospital in Madrid, he sometimes closes his eyes and thinks of the river, his grandmother’s bread and the smell of his grandfather’s workshop.
One day, he thinks, he will go back to live there.
And every time he thinks of it, he can smell the warm bread again.
